items.headline: SpaceX Starship reaches orbit on 14th test flight, deploying 26 Starlink satellites
items.title: Starship Reaches Orbit on 14th Test Flight
items.scifi_hook: A massive rocket reaches orbit, releases a fleet of broadband satellites in a single pass.
items.eli5: Starship flew to space, lost an engine, but still put 26 internet satellites into orbit.
items.why: Shows reusable heavy‑lift capability and expands global internet coverage.
items.text: SpaceX’s Starship reached orbit for the first time this morning. After 14 test flights, Monday’s effort is the first operational mission for Starship, a spacecraft upon which many in the space industry are planning their missions in the near future. Flight details: Starship lifted off from SpaceX’s Starbase, TX launch pad at 8:48am ET. During its ascent, the ship lost one of its six engines, forcing SpaceX to reconsider its orbital launch attempt. However, engineers ultimately decided to go, and Starship entered orbit ~25 minutes after liftoff. What’s onboard: After reaching orbit, Starship deployed 26 V3 Starlink sats over about 30 minutes using its ‘Pez dispenser’ system. While past Starship test flights have deployed Starlink, those past satellites were just for brief testing before reentering the atmosphere. Monday’s batch of Starlink is the first to be deployed by Starship that will join the full satellite broadband constellation and conduct normal operations. SpaceX officials said they made contact with the first satellites just a couple minutes after deploying them. What’s next: Future Starship flights will be able to hold up to 60 V3 Starlink sats. items.headline: Astronomers find ultra‑faint Fornax‑7, a possible satellite of a dwarf galaxy
items.title: A tiny stellar system may be a 'satellite of a satellite'
items.scifi_hook: A tiny star cluster may be orbiting another tiny galaxy, a cosmic ‘moon of a moon.’
items.eli5: Scientists spotted a very small group of stars that might be orbiting a dwarf galaxy.
items.why: Helps understand how small galaxies form and interact.
items.text: Astronomers using data from the Euclid space telescope have discovered an exceptionally faint stellar system near the Fornax dwarf galaxy. Called Fornax-7, it appears to contain only about 170 times the mass of the sun in stars. The discovery paper was posted to the arXiv preprint server on Sept. 13.

items.headline: Star Catcher readies Protostar for in‑space power‑beaming demo on Transporter‑18
items.title: Star Catcher’s Orbital Power-Beaming Demo is Ready for Launch
items.scifi_hook: A prototype will beam electricity between two fast‑moving spacecraft, testing an orbital power grid.
items.eli5: A new device will try to send power wirelessly between two satellites moving at 27,000 km/h.
items.why: Demonstrates technology that could power future satellite constellations without extra hardware.
items.text: Last fall, Star Catcher beamed power down a runway in Florida. Now, the company wants to try the same thing between two spacecraft moving at roughly 27,000 km/h. The company announced today that its prototype power node—dubbed Protostar—is prepped for SpaceX’s Transporter-18 launch, launching NET Oct. 1. Protostar will attempt to beam power between two untethered spacecraft for the first time—a critical step to scale Star Catcher’s orbital energy-infrastructure ambitions. The team aims to get an operational grid in orbit by the end of the decade. “This is our first time sending a prototype of our full core tech stack into space—testing this on orbit is success in and of itself,” Star Catcher cofounder and CEO Andrew Rush told Payload via email. Meet Protostar: Protostar will be the first end-to-end in-space demo of the company’s core tech stack: energy harvesting, satellite acquisition and tracking, and power transmission. During the mission, Protostar will deploy and track a cubesat, beaming measurable power to its off-the-shelf solar panels. The company claims customer satellites can generate two to ten times more power with no hardware retrofit. If successful, the test will validate commercial power-beaming operations. The team has already started development on Protostar’s successor—which includes a pilot power plant to beam operational levels of orbital power. items.headline: U.S. signals support for Brazil's critical‑minerals processing chain
items.title: US warms to building Brazil critical minerals chain
items.scifi_hook: America backs Brazil to turn raw rare‑earth ore into finished products, reducing China dependence.
items.eli5: The U.S. wants to help Brazil build factories that turn mined minerals into usable materials.
items.why: Secures supply of strategic minerals and encourages downstream investment outside China.
items.text: The United States is signalling a willingness to help develop Brazil’s critical minerals processing industry as Washington seeks access to the country’s vast resources while reducing reliance on China. US embassy sources told MINING.COM that American representatives have stressed in meetings with Brazilian counterparts that they are open to commitments that add value locally, including support for processing and refining. The message comes as mining companies with US ties increasingly consider moving beyond extraction in Brazil. “We have not excluded the possibility of building further downstream capabilities in Brazil,” a USA Rare Earth spokesperson told MINING.COM. Washington’s approach reflects a recognition that securing Brazilian minerals may require backing industrial development rather than simply shipping raw materials overseas. Brazil has made domestic processing a central part of its minerals strategy, raising the stakes for foreign investors seeking access to one of the world’s most prospective critical-minerals jurisdictions. Downstream push Caleb Orr, then-assistant secretary of state for economic, energy and business affairs, said in February that Brazil was a natural next step for investment in mineral processing. Former US chargé d’affaires Gabriel Escobar said in March that American investment in Brazilian critical minerals projects had already exceeded $600 million, with potential for billions more. items.headline: NASA completes tests on dual‑mode propulsion CubeSat
items.title: NASA tests dual mode propulsion CubeSat ahead of launch
items.scifi_hook: A tiny satellite can now switch between two propulsion methods, promising safer, more efficient spaceflight.
items.eli5: The CubeSat uses two different engines in one compact system, so it can maneuver without bulky fuel tanks.
items.why: It could lower costs and increase reliability for future small‑sat missions.
items.rationale: potential demand for versatile CubeSat services
items.text: Spacecraft propulsion traditionally relies on volatile fuels and separate, bulky systems for different types of maneuvering in space. NASA is working to change that. Engineers at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, recently completed a series of environmental and physical tests on a new small satellite designed to make spaceflight safer and more efficient.
